item.author: Scharon Harding
item.content:encoded: Since 2024, Microsoft has tried to sell “Copilot+ PC.” The marketing initiative was aimed at making it easy for people to know which Windows systems were approved to run AI-accelerated workloads locally.But Copilot+ PC branding is nowhere to be found on the new Surface PCs Microsoft announced this week.Speaking with Windows Central, Brett Ostrum, corporate VP of Surface, said that the new Surface computers “are not called Copilot+ PCs” despite meeting the label’s requirements.

item.title: Xi Seizes Trump Truce to Seek Lasting Gains on Trade, Taiwan
item.author: Colum Murphy and Nectar Gan
item.content:encoded: Donald Trump’s lavish welcome of Xi Jinping this week marked a high point for stability in a US-China relationship that’s seen a lot of lows. Now, the Chinese leader is pushing to lock in more favorable terms on Taiwan and trade while he still can.

item.title: We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rights
item.author: Simon Hattenstone
item.content:encoded: Despite attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failedIt couldn’t have been more prophetic. In 2008, 15 years before Manchester City were charged with financial fraud, fans started singing “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” to the tune of Yellow Submarine. This was because the former Thailand president Thaksin Shinawatra’s 15-month ownership of City had come to an abrupt end when more than £1bn of his assets were frozen. And although Sheikh Mansour of the UAE had stepped in to save City, we were sinking fast.Despite the UAE’s untold riches, by December we were in the relegation zone. It’s called Cityitis – shorthand for our tendency to self-destruct when things appear to be going well. In fact we won trophy after trophy. But we continued to sing the song about going down with a billion in the bank. When the financial fair play investigation was launched in 2018, the chant got louder. Then in 2023 we learned there were more than 100 charges. The chant became even louder and more cavalier. And now that our grubby, griftin’, cheatin’ chicken has come home to roost, you can bank on one thing (if banks still deal with us) – the chanting will be louder and more cavalier than ever.Continue reading...

item.title: Aaron Judge has the second-highest selling MLB jersey
item.author: Dani Mohr
item.content:encoded: To some, 99 is just a number. To others, it identifies one of the most well-known Major League Baseball players in 2026.Aaron Judge’s jersey, sporting No. 99, is the MLB’s second-most popular jersey this year, only behind Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers. Since Opening Day back in late March, Judge’s jersey sales have surpassed every other player in the American League, based on sales of Nike jerseys from the Fanatics network of sites, including MLBShop.com. They even surpassed former Yankee and now crosstown rival Juan Soto, whose jersey was the 10th top-selling this year. With Judge’s availability for the upcoming Wild Card Series in question, sales are sure to spike to support the Yankees captain. Postseason baseball will begin next week, and if you find yourself wandering around the Bronx or stopping by Billy’s Sports Bar, there’s no doubt you’ll find folks in No. 99 throughout a sea of pinstripes.

item.title: Gary Anderson: Breaking down Audi's colossal F1 upgrade
item.author: Gary Anderson
item.content:encoded: Audi should get the prize for the most comprehensive car update this season given how many new parts it has brought to Azerbaijan. However, it’s all about how it works together - and not just about a jumble of parts.Starting as always with the front wing, it looks like a completely new package. The mainplane now has a more defined upsweep going outboard, still integrated into the footplate of the front wing endplate, while the flap assembly appears to be loaded further inboard.Both of these changes will improve the consistency of the airflow going around the inside of the front tyre, especially when varying degrees of steering lock are applied.The increase in the three-dimensional effect on the leading edge of the front wing endplate will increase the outwash, as will the reduction in the camber of the blue-highlighted horizontal vane coming out of that endplate and the increase in size and detail of the small orange vane just in front of the tyre.Audi is more or less alone in that its front wing actuator is mounted on the wing’s upper surface. As opposed to hiding it, Audi has decreased its size.All of these developments could be grouped together as one development to better manage the airflow going around the inside and outside of the front tyre and wheel assembly.F1 being an open-wheel formula, the tyres are one of the most obtrusive blockages that F1 teams have to aerodynamically deal with. Changes in this area can have consequences further downstream, so these changes have led Audi into a very comprehensive update package.Audi's unique (until McLaren introduced its new sidepod package) sidepod leading edge and radiator inlet have also been modified in that there is now a slightly more bulbous section at the floor leading edge. This is probably to be more sympathetic to the airflow as it separates to go under the floor’s leading edge and/or around the side of the floor.The actual sidepods have also changed, with the upper surface now allowing more downwash and, with that, a change to the cooling exit system. Audi has gone from an array of louvres to a more common opening. This has required the magenta-highlighted section to be made into two sections: the front part with an opening at the rear and the rear section’s leading edge blocked off, which looks very bulbous.Continuing that theme of managing the airflow around the front tyres, the next question is - how can you optimise that new and revised flow structure? This magenta-highlighted outer floor edge doesn’t look very different. There seems to be a small more aggressive turned-up section just behind the bargeboard area; it’s simply a knife edge which should, because of the difference in pressure on the top and bottom surfaces, produce a vortex along its length, helping to seal that area of the floor.To complete this floor detail, Audi has also revisited the vanes in front of the rear tyre contact patch. This is in line with what I said earlier about managing the airflow around the blockage created by the tyres. Maximising the outwash in this area means there is less inwash, which disrupts the airflow structure to the diffuser, reducing its efficiency.Small details also count, as they all add up. This area of the intersection between the halo and the leading edge of the headrest can very easily create turbulence that affects the stability of the driver’s head. This small vane will help to consistently manage some of that turbulence.There are now four fairly large cooling exit openings. The cooling system works because of the pressure drop across the radiator cores: positive pressure on the inlet, negative pressure on the outlet. It’s very difficult to increase the positive pressure as that is generated by car speed, but a larger, better-positioned opening can fairly easily increase the negative pressure at the exit. The important thing is to minimise the downforce losses that any of these openings induce.Audi has also changed the angle of support that the diffuser sides are getting from these longer and repositioned floor stays that are highlighted in green.Nothing has been left unaddressed. The rear wing trailing edge trim details have also come under review. The aero, as with the cooling exits, is in reality circuit-dependent, so depending on the circuit requirements it can be altered as the race weekend progresses.The battle in that midfield is just as intense, if not more so, than the battle up front. Every single point has potential $ signs in front of it.Alpine introduced its big upgrade a few races ago, Williams came to Baku with a big upgrade, mainly a weight reduction - and now it’s Audi’s turn to air its developments. Who has taken the biggest step?Hopefully we will get an indication this weekend. Audi has not fared well so far - but Baku is a strange circuit.

item.title: These camera apps give you more control over the iPhone 18 Pro’s aperture
item.author: Andrew Liszewski
item.content:encoded: One of the questionable limitations of the iPhone 18 Pro's new main camera with a variable aperture is that you're limited to just four settings in the native iOS' camera app in manual mode: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. Those same limitations are also in place when the app is adjusting the iris itself in Auto aperture mode, but it turns out that's not a strict limitation of the iPhone's camera hardware. Apple's SDK allows third-party camera apps to implement more granular control of the aperture.

item.title: UCI Road World Championships: Ashlin Barry powers to under-23 men's title with 30-kilometre solo attack
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Ashlin Barry (USA) claimed the country's first ever under-23 road race title in the UCI Road World Championships, pulling off an audacious 30-kilometre solo attack from a five-rider breakaway that had already been off the front for more than 100 kilometres.Barry said he only went on the attack to get ahead and save some energy on the climbs for when the attacks came from the strongest riders."I didn't really think I would be strong enough to follow the the best guys on the climbs. Once I was away, I just committed. Honestly, I didn't think I could do it until until the last lap when I reached the top of the last climb. "Just complete disbelief, honestly."It was a massive birthday present for the dual Canadian-American citizen - the son of former pros Michael Barry and Dede Demet-Barry - who turned 19 today and was the eighth-youngest rider in the field. He gave North America something to celebrate after the region had been shut out of the under-23 men's medals since Taylor Phinney (USA) tied Canadian Guillaume Boivin for the bronze in 2010.Smiling for the cameras and waving to the crowds as he climbed to the finish, Barry crossed the line with his chasers well out of sight. It was 53 seconds before Hector Alvarez (Spain) out-sprinted the remnants of the breakaway for the silver, banging his bars in frustration, while Jesper Stiansen (Norway) took home the bronze.Barry lives in Toronto, and had ample support around the course as both the host country and the US fans who travelled to Montreal were cheering him on as he worked to hold off his chasers."It was just unreal being out there, seeing so many so many friends, seeing my family. I could hear my dog barking on the side of the course," Barry said. "It really felt like a home race out there. I just have to say I'm like so so grateful for for the support I had, and yeah, there's just so many people I have to have to thank."The result exceeded his expectations for his home Worlds, especially after he finished off the podium in the time trial."Honestly, I didn't didn't think it was possible," Barry said. "I thought maybe at best I could get get a medal or something or a nice result. I thought maybe in the TT - I could have a chance, but to to win on this course is just unbelievable."For Álvarez, third in the time trial, it was a difficult pill to swallow missing out on another world title."Ashlin was just stronger," the Spaniard said. "It was only me and the group against him, he was super strong and I need to congratulate him."I wanted to arrive at the front, but I have two [medals] - not the one I was coming for... but I am happy, in any event."Stiansen, however, was happy to reach his goal of landing on the podium."It was a crazy hard sprint and also a hard race - to come with third place is amazing. It was our goal today, but to do it, it's never easy," he said."It was full guys all day and crazy chaotic. Luckily, I found my legs during the last lap, so I could attack up to the front group, and I'm super happy to end it off with the third place."The under-23 men lined up under sunny skies ready to take on 13 laps of a 13.4km circuit for a total of 174.2km and 3,497m of elevation. The circuit started on the Avenue du Parc and include two main climbs: Camillien-Houde to the top of Mount Royal, Côte de la Polytechnique, and then tackle the uphill drag to the finish back on Avenue du Parc.Frank Ragilo (Estonia) made the first move early in the opening lap as the sun was just peaking above the skyscrapers of downtown Montreal. He was joined by Mads Landbo (Denmark), Filip Durdyk (Poland) and a rider each from Spain and the USA but the breakaway only gained ten seconds and was brought back before the end of the lap. There was plenty of action at the back, with riders getting tailed off, touching wheels and falling, or suffering mechanicals. Ben Wiggins (Great Britain) was forced to chase back on, too.Before the end of the first lap, Kristian Egholm (Denmark) followed his teammate's lead and attacked, pulling away with Viktor Soenens (Belgium) and William Heffernan (Australia), with Romet Pajur (Estonia) trying to bridge. Before the end of the lap, the breakaway had swelled to 13 riders with Enea Sambinello (Italy), Pierre Basset (France), Timothee Coudiere Cantin (France), Landbo, William Holmes (Australia), Halvor Dolven (Norway), Jaider Muñoz (Colombia), Dawid Lewandowski (Poland), Mil Morang (Luxembourg) and Alejandro Granados (Costa Rica). They were chased by Enaut Urcaregui (Spain) and Jaka Marolt (Slovenia) at 13 seconds, and the majority of the peloton at 50 seconds at the end of lap 2.When a powerful chasing group set off in pursuit, with Cameron Rogers (Australia), Noah Andersen (Denmark), Victor Loulergue and Ugo Fabries (France), Jasper Schoofs (Belgium), David Haverdings and Guus van den Eijnden (Netherlands), Samuel Novak (Slovakia), Ashlin Barry (USA), Ben Wiggins (Great Britain) and Patryk Goszczurny (Poland), the peloton quickly shut it down, and the race was all back together on the fourth lap.An attack then came from Samuel Novak (Slovakia), with William Heffernan (Australia) bridging across along with Mattie Dodd (Great Britain), Kristian Egholm (Denmark) and Ashlin Barry (USA).By the end of the sixth lap, the five riders had pushed their lead out to just over two minutes, but an attack from Dodd at the start of the seventh lap with 75km remaining, saw him go clear of the group and force a chase from Heffernan, Novák and Barry, completely distancing Egholm from the breakaway.The efforts were short lived and the quintet reconnected before the start of the eighth lap but their lack of cooperation had reduced the gap to 1:45.By the time they reached the ninth lap, a six rider chase group broke off the front of the field that included Matteo Scalco (Italy), Rémi Arsac (France), Matteo Van Huffel (Belgium), Max Brok (Germany), Jacob Bush (Great Britain) and Jack Ward (Australia) and were in pursuit.Egholm found his second wind and surged on the Camillien-Houde ascent with Barry bridging the gap. The pair gained a slim seven seconds on Dodd, Heffernan and Novák. However the remnants of that original breakaway were reabsorbed into a larger selection of 25 riders that formed behind, leaving Egholm and Barry out front with a 45-second advantage.With riders from Belgium and Switzerland setting the pace, the gap to the two breakaway riders was slashed to just 30 seconds with 30km to go. Barry took his chances and surged distancing himself from Egholm.With two laps remaining, Barry pushed on in front of a chase group of five: Matisse van Kerckhove (Belgium), Hector Alvarez (Spain) Guus van den Eijnden (Netherlands), and Cameron Rogers (Australia), with Egholm tucking in behind them. At the bell, Barry still held out hope with his gap hovering at 40 seconds over the quintet and 1:08 on the larger peloton.As his rivals behind began to look at each other to chase, Barry just kept powering ahead and only extended his lead to win the gold medal.Ashlin Barry (United States)Erazem Valjavec (Slovenia)Daan Dijkman (Netherlands)Marcis Shelton (United States)Bogdan Zabelinskiy item.title: Yankees Mailbag: Finalizing the playoff bullpen and speculating on third base
item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.If Jones gets to 15 home runs and 50+ RBI, any shot at ROY?It’s been a more productive season than most would’ve predicted for Spencer Jones this year, but he’s nowhere close to being in the running for Rookie of the Year. Jones has played in just over half of the team’s games and has contributed a slightly above-average 109 wRC+ with 0.9 fWAR, nothing to sneeze at considering his initial callup looked like he was going nowhere fast, but it isn’t enough to contend with the likes of Kevin McGonigle, the presumptive favorite, or even the other contenders like Parker Messick, Munetaka Murakami, or Payton Tolle. There’s a whole host of other names you could throw in the mix too before you get to what Jones has done this year, but that’s not to discredit the young outfielder. He spent most of the year as roster depth and didn’t truly “make” the roster until the Yankees had to break the emergency glass and start playing him regularly in August when he displayed a revamped stance at the plate that turned his season around. Now he’s in position to start some postseason games for the team, and depending on how healthy Trent Grisham is he might just get the lion’s share of them.Who would make your Wild Card Series bullpen at this point? Boone said he’s leaning toward either 11 or 12 pitchers.It’s make or break time for the Yankees’ postseason roster, and the biggest question mark of who will make the cut comes in the bullpen. The team will of course roster their three expected starters in Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Gerrit Cole, and the back of the bullpen are all locks placing David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, and Brent Headrick safely on the list. Carlos Rodón and Will Warren, the team’s two other starting pitchers, should immediately be next on the depth chart as the team could utilize both in relief during the Wild Card Series, though they’d likely prefer to keep Rodón ready to start either in this Wild Card Series itself instead of Fried or Cole or in a potential ALDS matchup with the Rays if they can avoid needing him. That gives us eight pitchers who are surefire picks, meaning there’s room for three or four more to contribute.Our remaining candidates are as follows: Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, John Schreiber, Michael Fulmer, Luis Gil, Bradley Hanner, Elmer Rodríguez, Brendan Beck, Yerry De los Santos, and Angel Chivilli. Some have of those last several names have jumped back and forth between the minor-league roster and The Show in the past week or so, but we’ll consider them. Carlos Lagrange is a wild card who was recently discussed, but pitching coach Matt Blake said that it was unlikely for him to make his MLB debut in the playoffs. Considering the other primarily minor-league options—Rodríguez, Beck, De los Santos, and Chivilli—have only made scattered appearances for the big league team usually in spot start scenarios, none of them are very likely to make it, but they are eligible and the team might need to call on at least one of them to make it through the final weekend of the regular season giving them a final audition of sorts. It’s not as if the Major League field has done much to separate themselves, as this is the portion of the bullpen Aaron Boone has done his best to avoid in anything resembling a close game.Hill is the most likely candidate of the bunch to make it, more out of a nod to his past success than anything he’s done this year as the magic of his sinker has disappeared leading to a 4.60 ERA and 5.92 FIP. While not as shutdown a lefty specialist as he’s been in prior years, he’s at least still good at dealing with southpaws and can be utilized if Boone sees a lane for him to come in and slam the door shut for an inning. On the opposite end, Schreiber has done wonders against righties and has been sharp in particular since getting picked up by the Yankees in August after the Royals waived him. I’d imagine he could work in tandem with Hill to parse through a middle inning stacked with a particular handedness should the starter get pulled earlier than expected before passing the baton over to the big three relievers.That leaves a scant few options for the one or two spots remaining. Hanner is a hard-out, as he’s given up a run in all but his most recent outing and looked every bit like a September mop-up man, and I’ve shared my thoughts on Luis Gil’s status with the organization previously: he did well in two outings against Arizona since that inspired a bit of hope, but his most recent appearance with four walks against Tampa was not ideal (he and Hanner were also demoted last night). Fulmer has not wowed in his trial run in New York either, leaving Yarbrough as the default winner here providing a potential fireman that could be called on to give them multiple innings in an emergency situation if a starter gets pulled extremely early while buying time for Rodón or Warren to warm up.If they do run 12 pitchers then I think one of the shakier choices might have a chance at winning that spot, but the depth here is extremely hurt by the front office’s gamble on converting their starting pitching excess into quality relief — Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers being unavailable has hampered that strategy, and their availability at the time played a big role in not acquiring any relievers at the Trade Deadline. The Yankees will have to play with the arms they have at their disposal, and hope that they’ve got enough in the tank to make it through a difficult postseason schedule.Any thoughts on Garcia or Rice working out at third base over the winter to replace McMahon?I don’t see that working out, as both have been pretty entrenched as first basemen should they take the field despite experience elsewhere. Garcia is unlikely to even make it back over to second base in pinstripes, so extending him out to a position he’s never played feels like an unreasonable request. As for Rice, catching appears to be fully off the table at this point, and his defense still needs work at first base as is — I don’t think he’d handle a transition across the diamond and frankly, another position change would only go poorly regardless of where they’d stick him. Anthony Volpe is out there looking for a position and was recently seen taking grounders at third, but I don’t think either of the sluggers are looking over there any time soon.McMahon’s fate is still up in the air, but it’s not impossible that the team moves on from him with only a single year left on his contract after this season regardless of whether Rice or Garcia could cover his position. I imagine part of the impulse to shift one of them over there comes from concerns about Aaron Judge and where he will play in 2027, given the rib injury that took him out for most of the year came from him making an all-out effort play in the outfield. The time for Judge to exchange his outfielder’s glove may come sooner than we’d like but I don’t think 2027 will be it, nor will he need to be handed the DH slot for most of next season. If all goes well, he can fully recover over the offseason and start fresh with perhaps a more conversative gameplan covering the field. His cannon of an arm can still provide plenty of value out there even if he’s a little slower picking up the ball, and at this point I think it’d be an acceptable tradeoff to ensure he’s out there in the field for the overwhelming majority of games.There is still a bit of a roster crunch down the road even if Judge isn’t in consideration for regular DH starts as Giancarlo Stanton is still in the picture, but Paul Goldschmidt would be coasting away either to retirement or another one-year stint elsewhere unclogging some of the logjam for playing time. Truth be told, I have no idea how the organization will balance all three of Stanton, Rice, and Garcia on the roster, but I think that might be a problem they told themselves they’d think about further down the road when acquiring Garcia. There’s a very real world where we’re seeing the last hurrah for Big G this postseason should he even be activated, which would be a shame given all the big moments he’s come through for them in October but at the same time it’s also understandable because of how predictable and lengthy his IL stays have become.

item.title: The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions | Editorial
item.author: Editorial
item.content:encoded: The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations Within days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly, around $1m a year per pair. Americans’ views of China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.It is telling that the announcement was one of the main takeaways of Mr Xi’s visit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.Continue reading...

item.title: SD Worx-Protime add more strength to their climbing roster with Axelle Dubau-Prévot
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: After four riders announced their departure in recent weeks, SD Worx-Protime are ramping up their recruitment with Axelle Dubau-Prévôt heading to the Dutch team in 2027.Though the 30-year-old Dubau-Prévôt only has one season riding at WorldTour level, and only returned to the road in 2025, she has competed in cyclocross, mountain bike and gravel, bagging top results in the latter discipline. She rode with some success on the road as a junior, then spent the 2017 and 2018 seasons riding at Continental level for Spanish and Belgian teams. Despite this, her 2026 season was hugely successful, with 10th place at Liège-Bastogne-Liège as her outstanding result on the road. In gravel races this year, she has plenty of top-10 placings, with third at the European Championships her most notable result."We are convinced that Axelle still has plenty of room for improvement," the team’s sporting director Danny Stam said, admitting they have been following her since the UAE Tour in February.“Precisely because we want to strengthen our squad for the Ardennes classics, she’s an excellent fit for us. As she had to ride many races in support of the team last season, we haven’t yet seen the best of her. There’s certainly still room for improvement when it comes to climbing.”Dubau-Prévôt admitted she is still new to the sport, saying, "It wasn’t until 2026 that I turned fully professional for the first time. Before that, I combined cycling with my job as a nutritionist. I knew I had talent, but I thought, ‘What if I went all out for it?’"After Liège-Bastogne-Liège, I got calls from several teams. I took a chance with Team SD Worx-Protime. I’ve been following this team for years. It’s a dream to now be part of it. It feels a bit bizarre: ten years ago, my career was more or less over, and now, in my thirties, I’m suddenly a member of one of the best cycling teams in the world."Dubau-Prévôt, the sister of 2025 Tour de France Femmes champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, is the fourth rider to sign with SD Worx this year, balancing their losses, and joins Kerbaol, Eline Jansen and Rachele Barbieri.Leaving the team are Marta Lach, Blanka Vas, Femke Markus and Julia Kopecký, while Elena Cecchini will retire after 15 years as a professional.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: What explains Mercedes' most dominant performance of 2026
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: George Russell's pole-winning margin at Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, 0.837 seconds, marked the biggest defeat for Mercedes' rivals in a 2026 qualifying session.Even with just one car in Q3, Mercedes managed to beat its previous benchmark, of 0.785s, from the season-opening Australian GP weekend.It undeniably has the best car and power unit package in Baku, but its rivals compromised themselves, making that gap bigger than it needed to be, as we explain.Verstappen was down on powerMax Verstappen's Red Bull topped final practice and was looking like Mercedes’ closest challenger ahead of - and during - qualifying.But that challenge failed to materialise, with Verstappen ending up eighth and a second and a half away from pole - his biggest time gap to pole of the season when he has set a lap in Q3.His returning team-mate Isack Hadjar ended up as the lead Red Bull, in fourth, over half a second clear of Verstappen, who believed the majority of the gap could be explained by a mysterious power issue."The whole qualifying we were down on power, it was consistently half a second down to Isack's car," Verstappen said after qualifying."For whatever reason, we don't know why that happened in qualifying. Then in Q3, the middle lap coming out of the last corner, my battery didn't go to 100%, so I had to abort that lap."And too cold tyres then, because you don't have the speed, you don't have the power that you should have. Then when I tried on my final lap, with no power, the tyres [being] too cold and a yellow flag, it's not happening."Verstappen encountered the yellow flags for Lando Norris's off in Q3, which also compromised him, so that 1.5s gap was far from representative.If Verstappen had been able to put his three best sectors together, that deficit would have been 1.014s. That gap would have been reduced further with a clean final Q3 lap, with Lewis Hamilton believing Red Bull has the second-fastest car in Baku."It's a shame...the whole weekend we're doing a good job, I'm happy with the car and then it all just falls apart in qualifying because of problems out of my control," Verstappen said."It's a little bit this season...it's a bit too fragile at times."The Red Bull drivers have suffered from an aerodynamic degradation issue all season but Verstappen said this wasn't present in Baku.Asked by The Race if he might sacrifice his eighth place on the grid to take a new power unit, Verstappen said: "First just need to figure out what it is [the problem]."Otherwise, if you have to run with that also tomorrow [in the race], it's not going to be a lot of fun. Let's see."Verstappen did rank 20th out of 22 drivers in the speed trap (306.3km/h) across the start/finish line in qualifying, 11km/h down on Hadjar and over 18km/h down on Hamilton, the fastest driver through there.Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies confirmed Verstappen's comments, saying his car developed an issue during qualifying that "got worse as the session went on"."Not only did it bring a large straight-line speed deficit, but it also made our life very complicated with energy deployment and tyre preparation," said Mekies, who felt Verstappen's eighth place was "sort of a damage limitation" in the circumstances and added that Red Bull would "change the faulty parts" overnight.McLaren's major straightline deficitVerstappen wasn't the only driver complaining about straightline speed after qualifying.Reigning world champion Lando Norris seems resigned to a difficult Azerbaijan GP considering McLaren's overall lack of aerodynamic efficiency and what he perceives to be a particular straightline deficit on his car compared to the sister McLaren of Oscar Piastri."The guys say everything's working as expected, but when you see eight tenths to the top, it's painful," said Norris. "Our time losses are in the straights. That's another area we just need to look at, because we're just a step worse to Mercedes in everything straightline-related."I've been comfortable in the car the whole weekend. My last lap I made a mistake and I paid the price, but I'm at a point in the championship where I kind of have to go for pole, or I kind of die trying. Of course, I paid the price for pushing too much, but it is what it is.“It's been tough, especially with my car. We have to understand why I'm basically having to push more than Oscar to try and make up for my straightline speed [deficit].”Team principal Andrea Stella said McLaren was investigating Norris's deficit and added: "It seems to be linked to the behaviour of the fuel injection, something that hopefully we will be able to or the adaptive systems should be able to improve [for the race]."It looks occasionally [like] the power unit generates a bit less power. But this is a specific phenomenon; it's nothing to do with the overall behaviour of the power unit."McLaren has brought a significant suite of upgrades to Baku, in an attempt to improve the car's efficiency - including a return for its revolving rear 'H-wing' that debuted at Monza - but Norris clearly felt further steps are needed to put McLaren in range of Mercedes."They have a very efficient car - they always have done for years," he added. "We need to take a big step in that direction if we want to be competitive in any straightline speed track for the rest of the season."But they also have just a good car in all the corners as well. They're just doing a better job in all areas, power unit and car."Stella agreed. "While we have the same power unit, there's a few differences and I think it's fair to say that their package, chassis, ratios, power unit itself, it just seems to be more effective when it comes to generating top speed."Hamilton rues Ferrari run plan and 'stupid tyres'Hamilton's furious weaving before each of his push laps in Q3 highlighted that getting temperature into his front tyres was a factor in his challenge for a better grid slot falling away."I was weaving to try and save my life, and I still couldn't get these stupid tyres working," he said afterwards after he ended up sixth. "Such a pain in the ass. We've got to bring back some good tyres."But tyre temperatures did not explain the full deficit to pole position as he ended up 1.3s adrift of Russell and nearly half a second behind Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.Instead, the biggest time loss came from Hamilton having found himself running at the front of a train of cars so he was left without a slipstream.Ferrari opted to change its run plan for Q3, doing push, cool, push laps rather than having a run and then changing tyres.But its strategy backfired when cars Hamilton was running behind in the train - such as the two McLarens and Carlos Sainz's Williams - all were stopping, so got out of the way.By the time things had shaken out, Hamilton had realised he was alone on track, more than 25 seconds behind Russell and simply towing his team-mate Charles Leclerc around.At one point, realising what was happening, Hamilton asked his team for advice on what to do - but then told them not to worry as he would "look on the TV".Based on what Hamilton had learned when he got a good tow in FP3 as he ended up third, the lack of a slipstream was very costly."It was six tenths," he said, when The Race asked how much the gain from getting the tow right was worth. "I didn't have one in that session."Leclerc did, though, having followed Hamilton around, and that helped him secure his spot on the front row, albeit still well adrift of Russell.Russell’s first pole position since the Austrian GP in late-June stands as his most compelling qualifying performance since his outstanding Friday and Saturday at the Barcelona GP.He pointed to a slipstream that he felt gave him a tenth or two extra on a qualifying lap that "all perfectly came together" in Baku."I've been feeling in a great spot this whole weekend," said Russell. "I felt confident, I felt hooked up. I'm getting more and more on top of this car and what it requires, and it's just all feeling more intuitive."Not that he believed this has come from nowhere. Asked whether he felt this represented a breakthrough, he suggested that wasn't the case and instead pointed to his improved form since the summer break."It's definitely just been perfectly hooked up for me this weekend so far," he said. "Me and my team have put so much work in to help me get on top of the limitations."Since the summer break it's been great and the performance has been substantially better than the results have shown."Inevitably, Antonelli's absence from the track after clipping the inside wall at Turn 1 in Q1 means Russell didn't have the opportunity to prove he would have maintained his form from the build-up to qualifying and outpace his team-mate.But Antonelli, who completed fewer practice laps than anyone after a hydraulic problem struck in FP1, with the resulting power unit change delaying his start to FP2, always seemed on the back foot."I did miss a lot of laps but in FP3 I felt pretty good," said Antonelli. "It was just a misjudgement, with the grip changing so much. An unnecessary one in Q1, and it’s a very good reminder that, like this, things don't go my way, so I need to do a much better job."

item.title: 'Anything other than gold would be a disappointment' – Ultra-ambitious Paul Seixas throws down the gauntlet for Road World Championships title
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: Paul Seixas may only just have turned 20 this week, but the young Frenchman is already aiming for the biggest goal possible in the Road World Championships elite men's race on Sunday – and he will have an entire team at his disposal to help him achieve it.Second in the GP de Montréal less than a fortnight ago, and a surprise bronze medallist in the elite men's time trial last Sunday, Seixas spent no small amount of time in the French elite men team's press conference earlier this week weighing up the considerable strength in depth of the opposition. In terms of possible winning scenarios for Sunday, Seixas said he had been working specifically in training on his sprints, which he feels could well be necessary for him to succeed. However, as he also warned, any battle for the victory after 270 kilometres is a very different beast to how finishes tend to play out after shorter races than the Worlds. But with his team backing him 100%, he said, and some great form, his morale going into what is only his second elite men's road race this autumn – he was 13th in Kigali last year – could only be high.Asked if he needed to finish solo to win gold, Seixas explained that that might not be necessary, due to the inherent difficulty of such a hilly, long race, with nearly 4,000 metres of vertical climbing."It doesn't matter which rider you are, they'll all tell you they prefer to finish alone because it's the simplest way of winning," Seixas said in comments reported by ."But finishing with several riders on Sunday could actually help me. I'm not the slowest rider in the world and I've been working on that [his sprint] once a week. That helps me maintain my explosiveness which can be important."At the end of 270 kilometres of racing, it's never the same. The finish is hard and we'll have to see about the wind direction as well."When it comes to being in the best position possible to take advantage of whatever circumstances Sunday throws at him, Seixas agreed that he felt complimented regardless at being given the role of sole leader for France."I know that I am physically capable of keeping up with the best, and the team is aware of that too. Do I feel the pressure? A little, but that is normal."Our ambition is simple: we want to win that title. Given my form, anything other than gold would really be a disappointment."Although Seixas was unable to beat Isaac del Toro (Mexico) on exactly the same terrain in the GP de Montréal, he did not feel overly troubled by the prospect of a similar scenario playing out again. His main concern, he explained, was to do with the pace of the competition, and keeping it as high as possible."What suits me the best is for the racing to be made tough," he explained. "We'll see how we do that, but we haven't had the pre-race meeting yet. [French team coach] Thomas Voeckler always has some ideas in his head about those questions, and I'm waiting to see what they are." "In theory, the Belgians are the top favourites, with Wout van Aert and Remco Evenepoel. They have two really strong leaders for two different scenarios, so it'll be up to them to control the race from the gun. But we'll see what we can do to challenge them."Just as Tom Pidcock argued a little later in the week, Seixas felt that despite having such a similar course, the Worlds would not be the same kind of event as the GP de Montréal."The long approach road to the circuit" – around 110 kilometres of racing – "changes things, and so does the lower number of laps" – 12 in the Worlds, 16 in Montréal. "To define what kind of rider can win on it, you'll just have to see how the course actually plays out. It's very open."Seixas said he had shifted his focus since the Worlds time trial completely, even if the bronze medal he took there was an excellent memory, to be sure that he kept his eye on what is the main prize: Sunday's road race."That's how it should be. I did the time trial well, but I've moved onto something else," he said. "I trained well, I've done some endurance work and I'm ready for the road race. My TT medal doesn't change things enormously, the two races don't have anything in common, but it does show I'm in good form, and that I've kept that good form in the last few days. "That gives me some more confidence for Sunday, but it doesn't change things so much."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: 'One final opportunity to give it everything' – Ashleigh Moolman Pasio set to close out 17-year professional career with World Championships road race
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: South Africa's Ashleigh Moolman Pasio is gearing up for her last outing on the road as a professional, with Saturday's elite women's road race at the World Championships set to draw to a close her 17-year career.The very last dance of Moolman Pasio's career will be at the Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Australia next month, she confirmed in a blog post on Friday, but Montreal will be her final road race as a professional.Turning 41 in December, Moolman Pasio has been racing on the European UCI circuit since 2009, gaining her first UCI contract in 2010 with Lotto Ladies Team when she was 24, and she's been a stalwart of the peloton ever since then, for a long time one of the only African cyclists in the bunch.Her career has spanned nearly two decades, and she's extended it multiple times in the last few years: she originally laid out her intentions to retire in 2022, then at the end of 2024, but extended her contract with AG Insurance-Soudal to bring her to the end of 2026.But first, there's the matter of closing the curtain on her own racing career."The preparation has not been completely smooth. I have not raced as much as I would have liked during the second half of the season, but I have continued to find ways to challenge myself. Racing virtually has helped me grow stronger week by week, push beyond my comfort zone and enjoy the process of building towards one final goal on the road."So, one last time on the road, I have done everything I can to prepare. I have arrived here in good shape, confident in my form and ready to give this final road race one enormous shot. I want to race bravely. I want to empty the tank. Most of all, I want to cross that finish line knowing that I gave everything I had, with no regrets."On Saturday, she will form part of a four-rider South Africa team, alongside Hayley Preen, Tiffany Keep and Lisa Bone. In some years, she has been South Africa's sole representative at the World Championships, but will line up alongside her compatriots this year, as well as riders from Mauritius, Zimbabwe, Eritrea, Rwanda and multiple other African nations."My racing journey will not be completely over - there is still one final adventure awaiting me at the Gravel World Championships - but Montreal will close an enormous and defining chapter of my life," she wrote."Then, I will be ready to move into the next one: using everything this sport has taught me to help pave the way for the next generation of African cyclists. To share my experience, knowledge and belief with young riders who may not yet realise what is possible - just as I once could not imagine what was possible for me."Moolman Pasio's career highlightsTwo-time Giro d'Italia runner-upFourth on the Tourmalet at the 2023 Tour de France GC wins at the Tour de Romandie and Emakumeen Bira12-time South African Champion (road race and time trial)Five-time African ChampionEighth at World Championships In her blog post, she shared various anecdotes and stories from her career, including the holiday with her now-husband Carl where he became convinced she could be one of the world's finest cyclists, and the decision to leave the world of study and engineering to pursue a career in the sport."After graduating, we took an enormous leap of faith and moved to Europe so I could try to build a professional cycling career. I could never have imagined where that decision would lead," she wrote."I never dreamt that I would compete at four Olympic Games, win mountain stages of the Giro, stand on the Giro podium multiple times, finish on the podium at Flèche Wallonne, win Emakumeen Bira and the Tour de Romandie, or become the first UCI Cycling Esports World Champion during the pandemic. I certainly never imagined that I would spend 17 years racing among the very best cyclists in the world."She also reflected on how her career has changed and evolved over the years, such as taking more interest in virtual racing during the pandemic, setting up the Rocacorba Collective and its ambitions to empower female riders, the biggest lessons of her career, and recovering from a broken back in 2024."Seventeen years ago, I arrived in Europe with a dream that initially felt far too big," she wrote. "Now, as I prepare to pin on a number for my final road race, I can look back with immense pride and gratitude. Not only for the results, but for the person this journey has helped me become, for the people who have walked it with me and for the community that will remain long after the racing ends."One last race on the road. One final opportunity to give it everything. No regrets."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Sainz penalised for second yellow flag breach in one day
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Williams Formula 1 driver Carlos Sainz has received a five-place grid penalty for ignoring yellow flags during Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying.The penalty denies Williams what was set to be its best grid position of the year, superseding Alex Albon's 11th place on the Monaco GP grid.Remarkably, the sanction came on a day on which Sainz was already investigated - and found guilty - of a different yellow-flag breach, although on that occasion he was let off with a reprimand due to mitigating circumstances.Sainz and Williams were originally hauled in front of the stewards after Friday morning practice for a yellow flag breach through Turn 4. The stewards ruled that Sainz "failed to sufficiently reduce speed" under the yellow flag - but felt there was sufficient mitigation to avoid the imposition of the grid penalty in "the very short period between the single yellow being displayed and Sainz entering the relevant marshalling sector".No such mitigation was present in a different incident, recorded during the third qualifying segment. In fact, the stewards pointed out that Sainz received advanced warning from the team that a yellow flag was out on the approach to Turn 3, and simply failed to heed it sufficiently.The warning in question was "yellow ahead, yellow ahead, [Lando] Norris, just do a lift, do a lift, and complete the lap" and then an apparent "clear-clear" that followed seconds later - seemingly creating a situation that led Sainz to believe the yellow flag was no longer acutely relevant."[Sainz] explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the yellow area as a whole," the stewards wrote as part of a lengthy explanation."He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a 'global lift' covering the consecutive yellow sectors. He further explained that the car [Norris] which had originally caused the yellow was no longer in the runoff area and that he expected the yellow flags to be withdrawn."The stewards did not accept this interpretation. Where consecutive marshalling sectors are subject to yellow-flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant reaction to reduce speed in each individual yellow marshalling sector. A reduction in a subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the preceding yellow sector. The obligation is also not dependent on the driver's own assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of the yellow sector."McLaren driver Lando Norris had indeed vacated the relevant runoff by that point - but as the FIA stewards do not want the drivers to self-assess the validity of a yellow flag, they found the lack of any "meaningful reduction in speed" in the relevant marshalling sector was sufficient grounds for the penalty.In addition to the five-position penalty, which demotes Sainz from ninth to 14th, he has also received two penalty points - taking him to a total of four for the 12-month period.Sainz was not alone in incurring a grid penalty after Baku qualifying.A three-position penalty has been assessed against Cadillac driver Sergio Perez for impeding McLaren driver Oscar Piastri in the opening segment.The stewards wrote that Perez "received two radio warnings" from the team but still forced a needless lift from the McLaren driver through the Turns 18-19-20 section, by "not managing his preparation lap in accordance with specific traffic-management instructions" - namely the race director's order that a driver on a prep lap stay to the right-hand side and avoid weaving in front of incoming cars.Because of the engine component penalties to the Aston Martin cars, however, Perez is only set to lose one position on the grid - going from 19th to 20th (the position he originally qualified in), behind team-mate Valtteri Bottas.

item.title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
item.author: Patrick Wintour in New York
item.content:encoded: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.Continue reading...

item.title: After seven years, a spacecraft company is releasing its Otters into the wild
item.author: Eric Berger
item.content:encoded: Imagine starting a space company in October 2019 with the aim of changing the world. Then, a few months later, a global pandemic shuts the world down."Little did we know what the world had in store for us," said Trevor Bennett, an engineer who co-founded Starfish Space after a few years at Blue Origin. "But that's kind of become part of our story, showing some resilience along the way."At Blue Origin, he saw, up close, the ambitions of billionaires to build big rockets and put massive numbers of satellites into orbit. Bennett and his co-founder, another engineer from Blue Origin named Austin Link, began to think about the implications. How would humanity deal with that increased volume of satellites in orbit? Could low-Earth orbit be preserved?

item.title: US being left behind in EV charging speeds as China goes sub-5 min to 70%
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: Hype merchants have a habit of overdoing it, but there’s no denying that China is making the US look more than a little antiquated when it comes to electric vehicles. Some of that is due to a deep integration of connected services and an extension of the car as part of the owner’s digital life—think additional infotainment screens and AI personal assistants, but with an Android phone-maker’s cadence of updates rather than that of a traditional car company. Other advances sound more appealing. China’s OEMs are in a battle over who can charge the fastest, and this week, Geely fired its latest salvo.China might have a much younger driving culture than North America or Europe, but it has still been long enough to condition those drivers to how long it takes to fill a tank of gas. For all their many improvements over internal combustion engine vehicles—far greater efficiency, instant torque, very little NVH, more reliabiity, and so on—EVs do still take longer to recharge than it takes to refuel a car with a liquid.At least until now, it seems.

item.title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma
item.author: Ben Doherty in Sydney
item.content:encoded: As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI raceWhen the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”Continue reading...

item.title: Winners and losers from F1 Azerbaijan GP qualifying
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: As a headline statistic, the biggest pole position margin yet around the streets of Baku points to an Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying session that might've lacked a bit of edge.The reality was very different - and not just because of the contrasting fortunes of the two Mercedes drivers.Here's our pick of winners and losers from Friday:Loser: Kimi Antonelli (16th)Given Mercedes' form so far this weekend, even with how compromised Antonelli's Thursday had proven this was still an easy (relatively speaking) 18 points just begging to be collected.That's still a plausible outcome, but it sure will be harder now after an "unnecessary" impact with the inside barrier at Turn 1 during the opening segment."I had a lot more headwind compared to the lap before, so the front just was much stronger, and I turned in roughly in the same spot, but obviously the car turned more and I clipped the wall," Antonelli explained.With 81 points in the pocket he can afford it - but there's no need to 'spend' a chunk of that margin this weekend. And maybe he won't - but he's put himself in a bit of a danger zone, in terms of grid position and the overtaking he will now need to do. Winner: George Russell (1st)Even before runaway championship leader Antonelli clipped the Turn 1 wall, Russell had been in formidable form. Without his team-mate for competition, that turned into pole position by a crushing margin of 0.837s.Russell described himself as feeling "hooked up" from the start of the weekend, and while Max Verstappen, who he described as "the biggest threat", was hindered by yellow flags and a worsening engine issue, Russell always looked on target for pole position.While it will take far more than one pole position, or even a victory on Saturday, to reignite his faded title chances, it's an important step in what Russell calls the "upward cycle" of improving his performances. Loser: Max Verstappen (8th)Max Verstappen reckoned he was losing half a second to Isack Hadjar because of an engine/power-related problem - and what was Verstappen's deficit to Hadjar in Q3? 0.581s.OK, you'd expect Verstappen (who topped FP3) to beat Hadjar with the half-second deficit removed, especially after Hadjar's three-race injury lay-off, and he might still have done had he not caught a yellow flag on his final run.On his second run prior to that, his battery didn't go to 100% for the run to the finish line, so that was another chance lost. Combined with the car's front-bottoming, which caused brake struggles, that meant a day that looked so promising turned into a nightmare for Verstappen. Winner: Isack Hadjar (4th)Ever a glass-half-empty driver in his time in F1 so far, Hadjar emphasised that with continuity instead of injury he would've "definitely" been on the front row here - instead missing out by 0.141s."Nothing outstanding," he added. But while a 2027 deal is already in his pocket it's certainly not a bad time to remind everyone, after three rounds of impressively workmanlike stand-in pace from Liam Lawson, that Hadjar has had serious speed this year.And he did admit he has been happy about how he's eased himself into this weekend, at a track that is just waiting to catch you out."I told myself it's mandatory not to touch the wall or anything. For a comeback, there's no point taking a lot of risks. So I was really driving a bit under the limit the whole weekend in that very tight section - I think I just did that natural step in Q3." Loser: Audi (17th and 18th)The two heavily-upgraded Audis had not impressed very much in practice - but even so, the double Q1 exit looks like an aberration.It's not just the power unit, Gabriel Bortoleto insisted."There were tracks like Monza where we were almost in Q3 and there are more straights than here. So I think it's something bigger that we need to understand," he said."I think it was better [earlier in the weekend], but still we were always on the edge of going out in Q1."The whole weekend we had no grip. If you don't have grip, you cannot go fast in the corners. If you don't go fast, you don't make a laptime. It's simple as that, and it's what other teams, when they go out in Q1, they probably say."Team-mate Nico Hulkenberg was more cheery, in relative terms, arguing his Q1 exit was "mostly because of circumstances", specifically a yellow flag and a lost tow. And neither he nor Bortoleto is suggesting the upgrade is misfiring - but certainly it's proving no game changer for Baku. Winner (then loser): Carlos Sainz (9th)Sainz put Williams into Q3 for the first time this year as its significant car upgrade excelled on debut - although Sainz felt the result was an overachievement.Alex Albon joined Sainz in Q2 as Williams escaped Q1 with both cars for the first time since July's British GP, which serves as evidence the FW48 is a more competitive beast in Baku.But Sainz (who does still face a yellow flag investigation) felt his ninth place was a result of Williams nailing its tyre usage and run plan, and "some serious laps on the limit" from himself, to end up a little higher than it would be on pace alone.He described the car as no different "in feel, just quicker" because it's lighter and has a bit more downforce - but the work done to achieve that has been immediately rewarded.Sainz admitted that getting a noticeable result felt pretty good for him, too, after a year spent toiling further down the midfield - and described the laps to achieve that as "the highest stress of the season" because of the challenge threading through the twists of sector two on a gusty day and low-grip track.What a shame, then, that a good deal of that good work was undone by a five-place grid drop for failing to slow for yellow flags. Loser: Esteban Ocon (14th)That aforementioned Hadjar lock-up in Q2 (on the right front, sending him into the Turn 15 escape road) had no real impact on his own qualifying - but did compound the misery of another French driver.Ocon had three tenths in hand over team-mate Ollie Bearman coming into their final run in Q2, but couldn't match Bearman with his first effort after returning to the track - compromised by what he described as a "gust of wind", which seemingly sent him onto the outside kerb at Turn 16."And then I did the same laptime, again, [before] arriving to Turn 15. I don't know who went off [Hadjar], but I had to back off on the exit to make sure that I was not going to get any penalty," he vented."I did exactly the same laptime. So yeah, I lost, what, three-four tenths? Unbelievable. You know, I just have no words. It's different race weekend, same s**t. It's always something going on, on my side, if it's either the car, if it's something else, now yellow flag, safety cars, whatever."But I don't deserve all the s**t that I have on my back at the moment. So I don't know, I might need to take a good shower." Winner: Alpine (7th & 10th)Alpine took full advantage of Antonelli's absence to get both cars into Q3 - a good day for any midfield team when the top teams usually hog eight of the 10 spots at the top of the order.Pierre Gasly managed to beat Max Verstappen - caveated by Verstappen's power issue, but still impressive - with his take being "great balance, great car, managed to get to Q3 pretty comfortably".Franco Colapinto had more of a struggle, and his off into the Turn 15 run-off, blamed on a flatspot, also cost Gasly on his final flying lap. Gasly reckoned sixth-place qualifier Lewis Hamilton was also there for the taking without that.A scruffy Q3, but it didn't matter, and Gasly's confident of keeping the rest of the 'midfield' behind. Loser: Sergio Perez (20th)The opportunity was there but, in the words of Perez, Cadillac "needed everything to go our way" to bag its first Q2 appearance.Everything did not go its way.Perez said Cadillac had the "wrong programme" in terms of how he and team-mate Valtteri Bottas prepared their laps. That went further awry when Bottas, who was due to provide the tow, was called to the weighbridge.Then Perez had his final lap wrecked by Fernando Alonso going up the escape road at the Turn 15 left-hander ahead of him (a chain of events that meant the Aston Martin outqualified the Cadillac). To add insult to injury, Perez has also been assessed a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri.The biggest shame is that we didn't get to see what Baku specialist Perez was capable of dragging out of the Cadillac. Because the form was there: 13th in FP2, 16th in FP3 - at the end of an eight-lap stint on the soft tyre on the latter occasion, too.The positive for Perez and Cadillac is that this wasn't competitive reality setting in. But not for the first time this season, they've probably been left frustrated by imperfections in their own execution. (To such an extent that a three-place grid drop for impeding Oscar Piastri doesn't make a great deal of difference.) Winner: Oscar Piastri (3rd)Although a front-row position was possible, as he was just one thousandth slower than Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, it was important for Piastri to get on top of McLaren team-mate Lando Norris after struggling in recent times.Piastri described it as "not an easy weekend" for McLaren, so felt third on the grid was "a really good result".Though he admitted that there have been some difficult laps amongst the good ones in Baku, overall he was encouraged with his own performance. "On a personal level, I feel we've been building up well," said Piastri. "I was pretty happy with my laps in Q3." Loser: Arvid Lindblad (15th)Racing Bulls's hopes of significant mid-weekend gains have not so far come to fruition - the car looked outmatched in qualifying relative to some of its usual opposition, and is at risk of a particularly bad points day on Saturday if the two Alpines ahead benefit from some classic Baku chaos.But while Lawson simply lamented the deficit on the straights, saying that Racing Bulls drivers are "trying to make up time that is not really there", for team-mate Lindblad such a quiet Q2 exit felt particularly sour."I'm a bit frustrated, more at myself than anything just because I feel that I didn't do something special like I normally do at the end of these qualifyings to put us in the final part," he regretted, admitting that his Thursday crash has compounded a shortage of confidence on braking."It's not been a good day, it's not been a good week. I just need to understand why I haven't been on it."

item.title: Hamilton frustrated after late Ferrari qualifying strategy change: ‘I towed Charles the whole time’
'Job's not finished' – Demi Vollering keeping quiet on game plan as she leads Dutch squad at Road World Championships
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: The Dutch women came into this Road World Championships in Montreal with a unique strategy compared to previous years; the nucleus centred on one rider. While it may seem obvious that Demi Vollering, the world's top rider, would lead the charge, it wasn't a slam dunk.The decision breaks from the multi-faceted options used in the past by the Dutch team. Vollering is a prolific winner, but she has never won a world or national title. But you can't ignore that she is a European Champion, has two yellow jerseys from the Tour de France Femmes and plenty of momentum coming into Canada."She is incredibly focused, that's true. Two days after the Tour de France, I got the first message already from her, 'OK, job's not finished'. I was like, 'OK, she's on'," Laurens ten Dam, the Dutch coach, told on Thursday evening."I think 10 days after the Tour de France, I saw her [at a F1 race] and I saw the fire in her eyes. It showed me that she's not done yet with the season. She wants to have this jersey for next season, so that's the most important."He said the team selection was made looking at all results, as well as how races unfolded. While there is no Marianne Vos or Anna van der Breggen [out with illness – Ed.], he said the team was solid and "Demi is the biggest chance of winning"."I think Laurens especially did a really good job with [team selection]. He had a lot of contact with everyone, and he also reported back to me. All the girls are fully on board with that," Vollering told a small media gathering, including , two days before the road race."We have a nice selection here and also really a luxury position representing the Netherlands. We have Anna [van der Breggen] out, of course, and Chantal [van den Broek-Blaak, retired - Ed.] is out, but in the end I don't necessarily think that we have a lesser team here."I really think that we have a very nice plan that is super clear for all of us, but of course I'm not going to tell you that. We can say afterwards, I think," she laughed.This year she lines up with Karlijn Swinkels, Riejanne Markus, Lieke Nooijen, Puck Pieterse, Amber Kraak and Femke De Vries. Last year, Markus was fifth in the Worlds road race, while Swinkels is in form, having recently won the GP de Wallonie."I also kind of like specific pressure, that all these riders are [supporting] you now. That ultimately gives me that extra percentage on the course later, during the race, to be able to finish it off, and I actually thrive on that. [It is] a bit of a sense of responsibility to also give the girls a reward for their work."The reigning European Champion goes back to work at her first UCI race since winning back-to-back Grand Tours. And before that, she dominated the spring with wins at Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, the Tour of Flanders, La Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège for a third time."I think I'm in good shape, but in the end, you only really start feeling that when you're riding around on the course and when you also see the competition," she said."I also think this is a course where, if you don't have the absolute best legs, you can still come a very long way. So even if the feeling isn't 100%, then you should never lose hope, because it's so long. I think it can really become a very interesting race in that regard."The elite women face a hilly 180.1km route that favours Vollering, with the closing Mount Royal circuit done eight times, featuring the Camillien-Houde climb.Her Worlds road race history consists of a silver in Glasgow, fifth in Zurich, and seventh places in Leuven and Kigali. She wants to add a rainbow jersey, but it is not ever-present in her mindset going into race day."Hopefully this is the reward, but we don't know; that is something we don't have in control. But what we do during the race, we have control, so that's more what I thought."This year I've shown that whether the climbs are shorter or longer, that I'm in a position to make a difference in different places. I definitely think it can be a Demi-course if it's just made hard enough."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Why an F1 2026 standout regrets 'trying to be too special'
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 rookie Arvid Lindblad delivered a scathing self-assessment of his performance so far at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and will adjust his approach after “trying to be too special”.The Baku weekend is proving arguably the toughest of Lindblad’s impressive first season in F1 as he crashed heavily in FP2 then made several mistakes in qualifying, which he ended slowest of the Q2 runners - his second-worst result of the year.Lindblad said the Racing Bulls car has been “bad on the brakes” all through practice and qualifying and “just not been fun to drive” but said he shouldered responsibility for misjudging how aggressive to be in practice and shattering his own confidence.His FP2 shunt, which was a result of taking too much speed into the narrow castle section and slamming heavily into the wall on the outside, came after crashing in second practice at the last race in Madrid too.It has left Lindblad running a slightly older specification of parts compared to team-mate Liam Lawson, too, after Racing Bulls debuted a new front wing here.“I have no confidence, to be honest,” he said. “Crashing yesterday, it doesn't help. I'm running a different car to Liam - as you'd expect when you crash, so that doesn't help.“I've missed mileage as well, I missed the start of FP1, start of FP2 and then I crashed, I missed basically all the rest of it.“I need to...I think there's stuff for me to learn on how to approach these weekends and manage them in a little bit of a better way because it's been two street circuits now where I've crashed in FP2 and hurt my trajectory to qualifying.“We were struggling this weekend so probably Q3 wasn't possible but I definitely think if I'd managed things a little bit better we could have been in a better place going into this session and maybe, with a little bit of magic on my side, could have been in Q3.”Lindblad said that not pulling something out of the bag was “what annoys me” most. He has started inside the top 10 for nine of the 14 grands prix – including the last seven in a row.“I'm just mad at myself because, more than anything, in trying to be too special I've hurt my trajectory for when it matters and I haven't delivered in the moment,” he said.“I enjoy being able to sort of switch off the brain and just send it when it matters and just go and have a bit of fun with it but this week I haven't really been able to do that and I think I could have just managed things in a better way to do that.”Lawson was only 12th fastest on a weaker weekend for Racing Bulls than the fifth-placed team in the championship has come to expect this year.He put that down to lacking engine performance compared to other teams in the midfield - and said that is partly where being on a knife-edge on the brakes has come from.“We're just trying to make up time that is not really there and it's really tough,” said Lawson.“Overall, if I look at my last lap of quali, it was the best lap I've done and with the right tow it would have been enough to get through to Q3, but that's pretty much everything going perfectly to plan and on a track like this that's obviously not happening for everybody.“We've definitely struggled all weekend, it's been tough, but I think it's similar to Monza. These tracks with these really long straights we suffer a little bit more now than we did before.”

item.title: With PRIMA, NASA will try to build a billion-dollar space telescope in record time
item.author: Stephen Clark
item.content:encoded: The first in a new class of space telescopes is on track to reach the launch pad in the early 2030s, NASA announced this week.The PRIMA mission will be the first of NASA's Probe Explorers, a new line of observatories intended to do more science for less money. The agency's space telescopes typically fall into lower-cost "Explorer-class" missions, with cost caps in the range of a few hundred million dollars, or flagship observatories like the recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which came with a price tag of some $4.3 billion.With the Probe Explorers, NASA officials seek to find a better balance between the smaller Explorer missions and multibillion-dollar flagships. NASA has studied potential Probe Explorer mission concepts for several years after an independent panel of scientists recommended the new mission category. But it wasn't clear until recently whether NASA's science budget, which is under pressure from the Trump administration, would be sufficient to actually start developing one.

item.title: CRO Race: Colombian Dani Martínez ends two-year win drought with small group victory on stage 4
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Dani Martínez (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) won an exciting fourth stage of the CRO Race on Friday, sprinting to victory from a group of five escapees which came together around 45km from the line.Louis Vervaeke (Soudal-QuickStep) was second, while Domen Novak (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) took third, having briefly been dropped on a short, late climb.Finishing in the reduced chasing bunch, 15 seconds behind the leaders, Tobias Svarre (Uno-X Mobility) continues to lead the general classification by four seconds, with two stages remaining.The leading group worked well to hold off the bunch, which trailed by only 30 seconds for much of the final 20km. However, their victory was complicated by the arrival of Sam Maisonobe, the Cofidis rider escaping the peloton inside the final 5km, catching the leaders and instantly opening the sprint.However, ultimately the Frenchman did little more than lead out the sprint from the break, with Martínez winning by almost two bike lengths.For stage 4 the CRO Race tackled another lumpy day, this time racing 160km from Lual to Rijeka on the coast.The opening 60km of the stage were frantic, with attack after attack coming, but no breakaway able to form. Only inside the final 100km on the approach to the day’s first classified climb, were Louis Vervaerke (Soudal-QuickStep), Lennard Kämna (Lidl-Trek), Gorka Sorarrain (Caja-Rural-Seguros RGA), Julius Johansen (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Samuel Boardman (Modern Adventure) and Mihael Štajnar (Pogi Team Gusto Ljubljana) able to build a gap.By the time they reached the bottom of the main climb to Učka, they led by around two minutes, though Vervaeke had slipped backwards.The climb was a beast, its 10.3km averaging at 7.7% gradient, with long sections well over 10%, and it duly took its toll. The breakaway split, leaving Kämna to ride on alone, Soraarrain trying to follow.By the time Kämna crested the top, the peloton were only 50 seconds behind, but with over 50km remaining that lead was allowed to grow, and as it approached 1:50, three chasers went clear. Domen Novak (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Dani Martînez (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) and Vervaerke quickly gained ground, and when Aimé De Gendt (Pinarello-Q36.5) joined them, there was panic in the Uno-X Mobility squad as Tobias Sverre’s GC lead came under threat.Sensing a threat to Antonio Tiberi’s second place overall, Bahrain Victorious came to assist, and when they were joined by Caja Rural-Seguros RGA, the deficit finally stabilised at one minute, with Kämna still 35 seconds ahead.With 15km left to race, Kämna was caught and dropped by the four-man chasing group, and with even more teams assisting the chase, the reduced peloton was little more than 30 seconds behind. But with much of the remaining distance on a technical descent, they maintained their advantage until Martínez attacked 6km from the line.That move saw Novak briefly dropped, but he reappeared with 1,500m to go before they were joined by Maisonobe for the final few hundred metres and the last dash for the line unfolded, allowing Martínez to claim his first victory since two stages of the Volta
